newsitem.title: INDIA: Profit-taking derails Indian share rally.
newsitem.headline: Profit-taking derails Indian share rally.

text.p: Profit-taking derailed a five-day rally in Indian shares on Wednesday after an early burst of buying pushed Bombay's benchmark index above the psychological 4,600 barrier, traders said.
"The market should have been stronger today, but it's come off," said Jaspreet Ahuja, head of sales at Caspian Research (India). "I believe there has been some local selling."
Traders said some profit-booking by local operators and institutions clipped the market's bull run.
"I am still not convinced that the market's going to come down sharply. Even if it does it will be a correction, which is good," Ahuja said.
The Bombay Stock Exchange 30-share index shed 27.07 points, or 0.60 percent, to close at a provisional 4,520.95.
Earlier the index charged past the 4,600 mark, hitting a 34-month high of 4,605.41 -- just shy of its all-time high of 4,643.31 set on September 12, 1994.
A Reuter poll of first-half company results ending June 30 for 27 firms in the BSE index issued on Wednesday also dampened market mood, participants said.
Steel, cement and automobiles were hit hard in the earnings forecast but the poll showed overall growth.
"The market took a hit after Reuters flashed the forecasts, but I think the market just needed an excuse," said a dealer at a foreign brokerage.

The net profit of cement giant Associated Cement Companies was forecast to slide 64.7 percent to an average 194.10 million rupees in the first half of 1997/98 (April-March) from 550.50 million in the year-ago period.
ACC shares skid 108.25 rupees, or 6.5 percent, to end at 1,564.0 at the Bombay exchange.
Steel Authority of India (SAIL) was forecast to show a net profit of 1.09 billion rupees, down 70 percent from 3.61 billion last year. SAIL shares lost one rupee to 24.75.
A decision by the National Stock Exchange to postpone the new account trade to Thursday also weakened market sentiment, with operators unable to build fresh positions, dealers said.
The NSE on Wednesday cut trading hours due to technical problems. Trading took place for only for 90 minutes and the settlement that normally ends Tuesday was extended by a day.
"People were expecting a spurt today, but the NSE problem is likely to slow down activity," said Purvesh Shah, chief trader at Nucleus Securities.
Trading for the new account begins on Thursday.

Analysts however said the bout of profit-taking did not spell the end of the roaring Bombay rally. The surge has pushed the index 47 percent higher, making it the best performing emerging market in Asia till the first half of 1997.
"There may be a little correction but not much. The basic direction is still positive," said Prashant Purker, head of institutional sales at Peregrine Capital India Ltd.
One key indicator of the market's inherent strength has been advancing issues beating losing stocks in the broader market, traders said.
"The rise has been fairly broad-based. It's quite fair to say that B2 (smaller capitalised) stocks have also moved up," said Caspian's Ahuja.
On Tuesday, the ratio of advancing stocks trounced declining shares by a ratio of over 3:1 -- prompting participants to believe the market was luring investment buying.
"That ratio is indicating that retail interest is really building up," Ahuja said. "I won't be surprised if the market did not hit the peak tomorrow. We still have some steam left."
